t.4.49.1: Then the monkey Hanumān, joining together with Tāra and Aṅgada, searched the caves and the dense thickets of the Vindhya.
t.4.49.3: While they were dwelling right there, that time passed by.
t.4.49.2: And likewise the caves all around, frequented by lions and tigers, in the rugged places of the lord of mountains and among its great cascades.
t.4.49.4: That region was indeed vast and hard to search, full of caves and dense thickets; there the son of Vāyu searched the entire mountain.
t.4.49.5: Gaja, Gavākṣa, Gavaya, Śarabha and Gandhamādana, each apart from the others yet never far from one another, went on.
t.4.49.6: Mainda and Dvivida, Hanumān and Jāmbavān as well, Aṅgada the crown prince, and Tāra, the forest-ranger.
t.4.49.7: Having searched the southern quarter and its regions covered with masses of mountains, overcome by hunger and thirst, weary and longing for water, they saw a great cavern overgrown with creepers and trees.
t.4.49.8: Then out came krauñcas and haṃsas and sārasas too, and cakravākas, wet with water, their bodies reddened by the pollen of lotuses.
t.4.49.9: Then, having reached that fragrant cave, so hard to pass through, the bulls among the monkeys became agitated in mind with wonder.
t.4.49.11: Then Hanumān, son of Māruta, who resembled a mountain peak and was skilled in the ways of wildernesses and forests, spoke to all the vānaras.
t.4.49.10: Though apprehension had arisen in them, those foremost of monkeys, mighty and full of vigour, approached that cave with excitement.
t.4.49.12: Having searched the southern quarter, its regions covered with a network of mountains, we are all exhausted, and still I do not see Maithilī.
t.4.49.13: And from this very cave, swans, krauñcas together with cranes, and cakravākas wet with water were flying out on every side.
t.4.49.14: Surely there must be water here, whether a well or a lake, for these trees stand lush and green at the mouth of the cave.
t.4.49.15: Thus addressed, all the monkeys entered that cave shrouded in darkness, and they beheld it, without moon or sun, a sight that made their hair stand on end.
t.4.49.16: Then, in that impassable cavern crowded with many kinds of trees, they held fast to one another and went a distance of a yojana.
t.4.49.17: Bewildered and thirsty, agitated and longing for water, they roamed about tirelessly in that cavern for some time.
t.4.49.18: Then those heroic monkeys, emaciated, with dejected faces and utterly exhausted, despairing of life itself, beheld a light.
t.4.49.19: Then, having reached that pleasant region, a forest free of darkness, they beheld golden trees whose radiance was like that of blazing fire.
t.4.49.20: Sāla and tāla trees, puṃnāgas, kakubhas, vañjulas and dhavas, campakas, nāgavṛkṣas and karṇikāras, all in full bloom.
t.4.49.21: They beheld things that shone like the newly risen sun, with platforms fashioned of vaiḍūrya gems, and lotus ponds of the hue of blue vaiḍūrya, thronged with birds.
t.4.49.22: It was surrounded by great golden trees resembling the rising sun, and by large fishes made of gold, together with tortoises.
t.4.49.23: There they saw lotus ponds filled with clear, tranquil water, and golden aerial palaces, and silver ones as well.
t.4.49.24: They beheld mansions with windows of burnished gold, covered with networks of pearls, with storeys of gold and silver, and adorned with vaiḍūrya gems.
t.4.49.25: There the monkeys saw, on every side, splendid mansions, and trees in flower and laden with fruit, resembling coral and gems.
t.4.49.26: They saw golden bees and honey on every side, and couches and seats adorned with gems and gold.
t.4.49.27: All around they saw costly vehicles, and heaps of vessels made of gold, silver, and bronze.
t.4.49.29: They saw costly drinks and flavorful honeys, heaps of divine and precious garments, and heaps of many-colored blankets and deerskins.
t.4.49.28: They saw heaps of agaru and of celestial sandalwood, and pure, edible roots and fruits.
t.4.49.30: Searching here and there in that cavern, the valiant monkeys of great splendour saw, not far off, a certain woman.
t.4.49.31: Seeing her, a female ascetic clad in bark garments and a black antelope skin, restrained in her diet and blazing, as it were, with radiance, they were greatly terrified.
t.4.49.32: Then Hanūmān, resembling a mountain, with joined palms saluted that aged woman and asked: "Who are you? Tell me, whose is this dwelling, this cavern, and whose are these jewels?"
